title: Can You Handle the Tracking Error? | Dimensional
author: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
text:
Perspectives Can You Handle the Tracking Error? By Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President Can You Handle the Tracking Error? View All Insights

Oct 08, 2026 2 Minute Read Currency USD Topic Equity Investing Investment Principles

Historical data show that small cap, low relative price, and high profitability stocks each have delivered a premium versus the market. Some investors ask why bother holding anything but stocks that check all three boxes. I respond by channeling Jack Nicholson in A Few Good Men: “You can’t handle the tracking error!” The average returns for these stocks make a compelling case for concentrating in them. US small value high profitability stocks returned 17.1% annualized from July 1963 to July 2026, more than six percentage points greater than the broad US market at 10.9%. That’s the difference between doubling your money about every four years instead of seven. Before getting too excited, be aware there simply aren’t many stocks fitting this definition. Stocks that are simultaneously small cap, low price-to-book, and high profitability are about as common as foods that are both healthy and delicious. As such, these stocks represent a tiny portion of the market. The size of this group means their returns often have extreme deviations from the market. Their annualized tracking error has been 11.8%. While tracking error is an unintuitive statistic, this should crystallize things: At their worst, small cap value stocks with high profitability underperformed the market by over 72 percentage points in a 36-month period. Applying insights from research on stock returns is like cooking with spicy peppers. Few people have the stomach for them on their own. But incorporating them as part of a recipe can enhance a dish, just like tilting toward higher expected return stocks in a broadly diversified asset allocation can improve outcomes for investors. Glossary

Premium: A return difference between two assets or portfolios. Profitability: A company’s operating income before depreciation and amortization minus interest expense scaled by book equity. Relative price: A company’s price, or the market value of its equity, in relation to another measure of economic value, such as book value. Small cap: Stocks with a relatively small market capitalization. Tracking error: A measure used to quantify how closely a portfolio follows an index or benchmark, often defined as the standard deviation of the difference between the portfolio and index returns.
